newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian tourism bodies angered by Sydney "bed tax".
newsitem.headline: Australian tourism bodies angered by Sydney "bed tax".

text.p: Australian hoteliers and tourism officials reacted angrily on Tuesday to news that New South Wales state would impose a 10 percent "bed tax" on central Sydney hotels from September this year.

The tax, announced in Tuesday's state budget, is designed to raise A$64 million (US$50 million) a year. NSW Treasurer Michael Egan said in his budget speech that Sydney "has been almost the only great city of the world without such a tax".
But national and state tourist authorities, who are banking on the 2000 Sydney Olympics to create a tourist boom, said it would put the city at a competitive disadvantage at a key time.

"We are very disappointed with the news that the NSW government has introduced a bed tax, as we believe this to be the thin end of the wedge," said John Morse, managing director of the official Australian Tourist Commission.
"A bed tax will cost Australia jobs and investment -- pure and simple," added Bruce Baird, head of the industry body Tourism Council Australia.

"With the stroke of a pen numerous investment and development projects today have become unviable. The tax will also undermine profitability in the sector at a time when hotelliers and others in the industry are just starting to recover."
Hoteliers said they were appalled by the decision and felt betrayed after receiving informal assurances that no such tax was planned.
The Australian Hotels Association (AHA) said it would hold a crisis meeting on Wednesday to oppose the tax, which it said would add millions to the cost of the Olympics.
"The sad part is that accommodation drives the tourism industry," said AHA chief executive David Charles.
"If the tourism industry suffers a downturn, thousands of small businesses involved in tourism, including suppliers, will be drastically affected."
